city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.t_rec: Record highs and lows, by the decade that set them
text.p_rec: If Trenton's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Trenton has set 38 standing record lows, fewer than the 69 that chance alone would give, and 91 record highs, more than the 64 that chance alone would give. The 1990s hold the most record highs of any decade (48). Trenton's all-time high is 106°F, on July 9, 1936.
text.t_chg: Trenton's nights have warmed since 1986. Its days warmed over the long run.
text.p_chg: Across 130 complete years: Trenton's average low shows no clear change: −0.02°F per decade, a range (−0.09 to +0.04) that includes zero. Trenton's average high has risen +0.14°F per decade (95% range +0.07 to +0.20), about +1.8°F since 1893. The last 40 years tell a different story: since 1986, lows have risen +1.00°F per decade (95% range +0.67 to +1.32) and highs show no clear change. The full record joins different observing sites over the years, and a move (for example, from the city to a cooler airport) can hide or exaggerate a long-run trend, so the recent decades are the clearer guide here.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in none; 3 months fell. Highs rose in 8 of 12 months.

text.p_rain: Trenton's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (−0.08 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 46.5 inches a year. The wettest year was 1996 (67.46 in); the driest, 1957 (28.79 in).
